one_liner: Pure-Go ports of Vigna's xorshift/xoroshiro/xoshiro and SplitMix64 generators; raw calls 2-3x faster than math/rand's default source.
what_it_does: Thirteen small Go packages (splitmix64, xorshift64star, xorshift128plus, xorshift1024star, xorshift1024starphi, xorshift4096star, xoroshiro128plus, xoroshiro128starstar and the 256/512-bit variants) each expose NewSource(seed int64) returning a concrete type with Seed, Uint64 and Int63, plus Jump on most. Every generator satisfies math/rand's Source64, so it can be passed to rand.New() as a drop-in source; the root package defines XorShift and XorShiftExt interfaces for switching generators. Multi-word states are filled from SplitMix64 as Vigna recommends.
how_it_is_fast: The generators are linear xorshift / xor-rotate-shift-rotate recurrences over a few 64-bit words, costing a handful of shifts, xors and one add or multiply per output; the benchmark compares them with math/rand's default source called through the rand.Source interface (its internals were not inspected here). The 2020 rewrite switched to math/bits.RotateLeft64, which Vigna suggested in issue #3 because the standard function can be intrinsified by the compiler, and the 256/512-bit variants copy the state into locals because, per a source comment, the Go compiler generated slower code for array indexing.
when_to_use: Go code (not C++) that calls Uint64() directly on a concrete generator in a hot loop, e.g. Monte Carlo or simulation inner loops, where the README shows 1.6-2.7 ns/op versus 4.93 ns/op for math/rand's source on an i7-3840QM.
Go programs pinned to an older toolchain (go 1.9+ per go.mod) that lack math/rand/v2 and want a small MIT-licensed SplitMix64 or xoshiro256** source.
Single-goroutine code, or one generator per goroutine, since nothing is locked.
As readable reference code for porting Vigna's generators, after checking each one against the reference outputs (see gotchas).
when_not_to_use: From C or C++: it is a Go package; use Vigna's reference C code or a catalogued C/C++ generator instead.

Through rand.Rand (rand.New(src).Float64/ExpFloat64 etc.): the README's wrapped rows gain only about 1.2x (8.1-8.7 ns versus 10.2 ns), and the 256- and 512-bit variants are slower than math/rand (11.7-13.6 ns).
When you need Jump() to create non-overlapping parallel streams with xoroshiro128plus or xoroshiro512starstar: both have defects (see gotchas).
Concurrent use of one generator: README says it is not concurrency-safe.
Security-sensitive randomness: none of these generators is cryptographic.

integration.min_toolchain: Go 1.9 (go.mod 'go 1.9'; math/bits.RotateLeft64 needs 1.9); benchmarked on Go 1.14
integration.platforms: any platform Go supports (pure Go, no assembly)
integration.thread_safety: not concurrency-safe; the README says to wrap a generator with a monitor goroutine
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: every generator implements rand.Source64, so rand.New(xorshift128plus.NewSource(seed)) replaces rand.New(rand.NewSource(seed)), but the output stream differs and the wrapped speedup is small

gotchas: xoroshiro512starstar's state update is written 's6 ^ ^s7 ^ s3'; in Go the second '^' is unary bitwise NOT, so it complements s7, unlike the repo's own xoroshiro512plus ('s6 ^ s7 ^ s3') which shares the same xoshiro512 engine. The 512** generator therefore does not reproduce Vigna's xoshiro512** sequence and its Jump polynomial no longer applies (read in source; not run).

xoroshiro128plus uses the original 2016 parameters (rotl 55, shift 14, rotl 36, as in sysbench's copy of Vigna's code) but its Jump() uses internal.Jump128 = {0x8a5cd789635d2dff, 0x121fd2155c472f96}, the xorshift128+ jump constants that XorShift128Plus.Jump also uses; Vigna's jump for this xoroshiro128+ is {0xbeac0467eba5facb, 0xd86b048b86aa9922}, so Jump() is not the advertised 2^64-step jump. The repo's xoroshiro128starstar uses the newer 24/16/37 parameters and the matching jump constants.

The packages are named 'xoroshiro256*' and 'xoroshiro512*' but implement Vigna's xoshiro256/xoshiro512 engines (the 256-bit update and jump constants match xoshiro256); look them up under xoshiro. Package docs also call 256++ a 'floating-point' generator although ++ and ** are Vigna's all-purpose scramblers.

Int63() masks off the top bit (keeping the weak low bits) for most generators; only the + scramblers xoroshiro128plus/256plus/512plus were changed in 2020 to return the upper 63 bits after Vigna's issue #1. Vigna also reported a jump operator-precedence bug (issue #2, fixed 2020-02-27) and recommended reference-output unit tests, which the repo still lacks (xorshift_test.go has only benchmarks). The README example code does not compile as written (xorshift256plus.NewSource, unqualified XorShiftExt, rand not imported).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Among Go siblings, pick pgregory.net/rand (flyingmutant/rand, sfc64, maintained, measured against math/rand/v2) for a modern faster rand.Rand replacement and valyala/fastrand for many goroutines sharing an RNG; pick this only if you specifically want a Vigna generator family in pure Go on an old toolchain and can audit the variant you use. C++ users should take the C/C++ siblings (e.g. simdrng, Xoshiro256PlusSIMD, testingRNG's lehmer64/aesctr) instead.
verified_claims_summary: The author's go test -bench run (Go 1.14, default flags, i7-3840QM, Fedora 31, 2020) measured raw Uint64 calls at 1.61 ns (SplitMix64) to 2.66 ns (128-bit-state generators) versus 4.93 ns for math/rand.NewSource(...).Int63 called through the Source interface, so about 2-3x, partly from static versus interface dispatch; wrapped in rand.Rand for ExpFloat64 the best variants are about 1.2x faster (8.10-8.66 ns versus 10.2 ns) and the 256/512-bit variants are slower. math/rand/v2 was not measured.
status_note: Abandoned since 2020-05-02 (44 commits; the only three issues, filed by Vigna on 2020-01-30, were fixed 2020-02-27) but MIT-licensed, dependency-free and tiny; vendor only the generator you need and test it against Vigna's reference outputs first, avoiding xoroshiro512starstar and xoroshiro128plus.Jump as written.
